debate.situation: You are the one who proposes the plans. When you and your friend meet, it is lovely, but if you stop texting, the friendship goes quiet. You are weighing whether to say something. What you have reported is the pattern; why your friend does not initiate is unknown, and that is the decisive uncertainty. It could be habit, busyness, or lower priority, and the pattern alone cannot tell these apart.

minds.title: The Plain Speaker
minds.concern: Unspoken resentment and guessing games erode closeness; honest, non-blaming requests keep it alive.
minds.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg

minds.title: The Anti-Bookkeeper
minds.concern: Friendship is valued for itself, and keeping score can damage the very thing you are trying to protect.
minds.author: Michel de Montaigne

minds.title: The Maintenance Realist
minds.concern: Friendships need steady contact to survive, so someone has to carry the effort, and the cost should be sustainable.
minds.author: Robin Dunbar
minds.book: Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships

debate.speaker: The Plain Speaker
debate.text: Yes, say something, and soon. A pattern you are quietly counting is already in the friendship, just unspoken. I would not accuse. I would say what you notice and how it feels, then make one small request.
debate.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
debate.basis: Basis: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication

debate.speaker: The Anti-Bookkeeper
debate.text: Careful. The moment you say you always plan, you have opened a ledger, and ledgers are poison to friendship. The meetings are lovely; that is the evidence that matters. Perhaps she is simply no good at initiating, and loves you anyway.
debate.author: Michel de Montaigne

debate.speaker: The Maintenance Realist
debate.text: You are both half right. Friendships fade without contact, however warm the last meeting was, so the texting is not trivia, it is the upkeep. But the ledger point stands: the question is whether you can keep carrying it without souring.
debate.author: Robin Dunbar
debate.book: Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships

debate.speaker: The Plain Speaker
debate.text: I concede the audit is a bad idea. But you are already counting, or you would not be asking. Naming a feeling is not sending a bill. Telling her you miss her reaching out and asking her to pick the next day is a request, not a verdict.
debate.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
debate.basis: Basis: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication

debate.speaker: The Anti-Bookkeeper
debate.text: A request squeezed out of someone is a poor gift. If she plans because you asked, you will wonder whether she wanted to. Better to wait and see, or even stop texting for a while. Silence is a plain answer.
debate.author: Michel de Montaigne

debate.speaker: The Maintenance Realist
debate.text: Going silent is a blunt test with a muddy result. If she is busy or forgetful, you lose months of contact and learn nothing. The fact that would most reorder this: does she ever reach out in other ways, such as replying eagerly, sharing news, saying she misses you? If yes, speak lightly; if no, speak more directly.
debate.author: Robin Dunbar
debate.book: Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships

debate.speaker: The Plain Speaker
debate.text: Notice what else is unknown: what is driving you. It could be fairness, a fear of mattering less, or plain tiredness from the work. Fairness calls for a request about sharing. Fear calls for asking about the friendship itself. Tiredness might just need a lighter schedule.
debate.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
debate.basis: Basis: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication

debate.speaker: The Anti-Bookkeeper
debate.text: I would bet on the fear, though that is only a guess and she can overrule it. And she is pulled two ways: she wants this friend and she wants it to be fair. I will not rank those for her. Which weighs more is hers to say.
debate.author: Michel de Montaigne

debate.speaker: The Maintenance Realist
debate.text: Then start smaller than a talk. Say something warm and light, then hand her the next choice: your turn to pick the day. That costs little, tests willingness, and keeps the friendship in contact. I am extending Dunbar here; he does not prescribe scripts.
debate.author: Robin Dunbar
debate.book: Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships

debate.speaker: The Plain Speaker
debate.text: Fine as a first step, with a warning. A hint is not a request, and hints get missed. If nothing changes after one clear, kind ask, the fuller conversation is warranted, and then her answer is real information.
debate.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
debate.basis: Basis: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication

debate.speaker: The Anti-Bookkeeper
debate.text: I accept one clear, kind ask. Where I still disagree: some friends are simply the ones who are visited, and perhaps this is one of them. If the hours together are lovely, that may be payment enough. Whether it is enough is for you to decide.
debate.author: Michel de Montaigne

debate.clearer: The main insight is that the choice is probably not between speaking up and staying silent. It is between a heavy, ledger-like complaint and a light, specific ask that also shows how your friend responds. The minds disagreed about whether lovely meetings are enough on their own. They also left open whether your motive is fairness, fear of mattering less, or tiredness; each leads to a different ask. You might reflect on what you would want to be true after saying something: more balance, reassurance, or less workload.
debate.dependsOn: If your friend shows interest in other ways (replying warmly, sharing news, saying she misses you), a light ask such as your turn to pick the day is reasonable, because the pattern is more likely habit than indifference. If she is rarely warm outside meetups and the ask changes nothing, a direct, kind conversation about what you need becomes more reasonable, because her answer then tells you where you stand. If the meetings alone feel like enough and the effort does not tire you, continuing as you are is also defensible, because the friendship may simply run on your initiative. The decisive unknown is why she does not initiate. A proportionate way to learn it is one clear, friendly ask and watching what she does next, rather than going silent for months.
